Formed in 1876 and 1901, respectively, the NL and AL cemented their cooperation with the National Agreement in 1903, making MLB the oldest major professional sports league in the United States and Canada.[[14]](#cite_note-14)[[15]](#cite_note-15) They remained legally separate entities until 2000, when they merged into a single organization led by the [commissioner of baseball](/wiki/Commissioner_of_baseball "Commissioner of baseball").[[3]](#cite_note-MLBCommissioner-3)[[7]](#cite_note-AboutMLB-7)[[16]](#cite_note-2000nl-16)[[4]](#cite_note-Chass-4) Baseball's first all-professional team, the [Cincinnati Red Stockings](/wiki/Cincinnati_Red_Stockings "Cincinnati Red Stockings"), was founded in 1869.[[17]](#cite_note-17)[[18]](#cite_note-18) The first few decades of professional baseball saw rivalries between leagues, and players often jumped from one team or league to another.[[19]](#cite_note-19) These practices were essentially ended by the National Agreement of 1903, in which AL and NL agreed to respect each other's player contracts, including the contentious [reserve clause](/wiki/Reserve_clause "Reserve clause"), which bound players to their teams.

The period from about 1900 to 1920 was the [dead-ball era](/wiki/Dead-ball_era "Dead-ball era"), when [home runs](/wiki/Home_run "Home run") were rarely hit.[[20]](#cite_note-:4-20) Professional baseball was rocked by the [Black Sox Scandal](/wiki/Black_Sox_Scandal "Black Sox Scandal"), a conspiracy to [fix](/wiki/Match_fixing "Match fixing") the [1919 World Series](/wiki/1919_World_Series "1919 World Series"). Baseball survived the scandal, albeit with major changes in its governance, as the relatively weak National Commission was replaced with a powerful commissioner of baseball with near-unlimited authority over the sport. MLB rose in popularity in the decade following the Black Sox Scandal, and unlike major leagues in other sports, it endured the [Great Depression](

[Formula One](/wiki/Formula_One "Formula One") is particularly popular in the United Arab Emirates, and a Grand Prix is annually held at the [Yas Marina Circuit](/wiki/Yas_Marina_Circuit "Yas Marina Circuit") in [Yas Island](/wiki/Yas_Island "Yas Island") in Abu Dhabi. The race takes place in the evening, and was the first ever Grand Prix to start in daylight and finish at night.[[389]](#cite_note-393) Other popular sports include [camel racing](/wiki/Camel_racing "Camel racing"), [falconry](/wiki/Falconry "Falconry"), [endurance riding](/wiki/Endurance_riding "Endurance riding"), and [tennis](/wiki/Tennis "Tennis").[[390]](#cite_note-394) The emirate of [Dubai](/wiki/Dubai "Dubai") is also home to two major [golf](/wiki/Golf "Golf") courses: the Dubai Golf Club and [Emirates Golf Club](/wiki/Emirates_Golf_Club "Emirates Golf Club").

Aside from the leisure aspect, sports can play an important part in shaping national identity. Falconry, for example, has functioned as a national symbol since its inception in 1971.[[391]](#cite_note-395) Aside from the national prevalence of falconry, the UAE have played a formative role internationally in the co-ordination of [UNESCO](/wiki/UNESCO "UNESCO")'s recognition of falconry as [intangible heritage](/wiki/Intangible_heritage "Intangible heritage").[[392]](#cite_note-396)

Since 1785, twenty-two men have served as the institution's president, beginning with [Jacob Rutsen Hardenbergh](/wiki/Jacob_Rutsen_Hardenbergh "Jacob Rutsen Hardenbergh"), a Dutch Reformed minister who was responsible for establishing the college.[[60]](#cite_note-60)[[61]](#cite_note-FruscianoLeadership-61) Before 1930, most of the university's presidents were clergy affiliated with Christian denominations in the [Reformed tradition](/wiki/Calvinism "Calvinism").[[61]](#cite_note-FruscianoLeadership-61)[[62]](#cite_note-RutgersLeadersPastPresidents-62) Two presidents were alumni of Rutgers College—[William H. S. Demarest](/wiki/William_Henry_Steele_Demarest "William Henry Steele Demarest") (Class of 1883) and [Philip Milledoler Brett](/wiki/Philip_Milledoler_Brett "Philip Milledoler Brett") (Class of 1892).[[63]](#cite_note-63)[[64]](#cite_note-64)

The president serves in an *[ex officio](/wiki/Ex_officio "Ex officio")* capacity as a presiding officer within the university's 59-member board of trustees and its eleven-member board of governors,[[65]](#cite_note-65) and is appointed by these boards to oversee the day-to-day operations of the university across its campuses. He is charged with implementing "board policies with the help and advice of senior administrators and other members of the university community."[[66]](#cite_note-66) The president is responsible only to those two governing boards—there is no oversight by state officials.[[67]](#cite_note-67)

**Bahrain**,[[a]](#cite_note-17) officially the **Kingdom of Bahrain**,[[b]](#cite_note-18) is an [island country](/wiki/Island_country "Island country") in [West Asia](/wiki/West_Asia "West Asia"). Situated near the western shore of the [Persian Gulf](/wiki/Persian_Gulf "Persian Gulf") and latitudinally about two-thirds the shore's length from the north, the country comprises a small [archipelago](/wiki/Archipelago "Archipelago") of 33 natural islands and an additional 50 [artificial islands](/wiki/Artificial_island "Artificial island"), centered on [Bahrain Island](/wiki/Bahrain_Island "Bahrain Island"), which makes up around 80 percent of the country's landmass. Bahrain is situated between [Qatar](/wiki/Qatar "Qatar") and the northeastern coast of [Saudi Arabia](/wiki/Saudi_Arabia "Saudi Arabia"), to which it is connected by the [King Fahd Causeway](/wiki/King_Fahd_Causeway "King Fahd Causeway"). The population is 1,588,670 as of 2024, of whom 739,736 (46.6% of the population) are Bahraini nationals, and 848,934 are expatriates (53.4% of the population).[[2]](#cite_note-Census2020-2) Bahrain spans some 760 square kilometres (290 sq mi)[[17]](#cite_note-19) and is the [third-smallest nation](/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_area "List of countries and dependencies by area") in Asia after [Maldives](/wiki/Maldives "Maldives") and [Singapore](/wiki/Singapore "Singapore").[[18]](#cite_note-20) The capital and largest city is [Manama](/wiki/Manama "Manama").

[![refer to caption](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/42/Wien_-_OPEC-Zentrale_%28b%29.JPG/250px-Wien_-_OPEC-Zentrale_%28b%29.JPG)](/wiki/File:Wien_-_OPEC-Zentrale_(b).JPG)

OPEC headquarters in Vienna

The following month, during 10–14 September 1960, the Baghdad Conference was held at the initiative of Tariki, Pérez Alfonzo, and Iraqi prime minister [Abd al-Karim Qasim](/wiki/Abd_al-Karim_Qasim "Abd al-Karim Qasim"), whose country had skipped the 1959 congress.[[44]](#cite_note-:0-44) Government representatives from Iran, Iraq, Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and Venezuela met in [Baghdad](/wiki/Baghdad "Baghdad") to discuss ways to increase the price of crude oil produced by their countries, and ways to respond to unilateral actions by the MOCs. Despite strong US opposition: "Together with Arab and non-Arab producers, Saudi Arabia formed the Organization of Petroleum Export Countries (OPEC) to secure the best price available from the major oil corporations."[[45]](#cite_note-45)

The Middle Eastern members originally called for OPEC headquarters to be in Baghdad or Beirut. Venezuela argued for a neutral location, and so the organization chose [Geneva](/wiki/Geneva "Geneva"), Switzerland. On 1 September 1965, OPEC moved to [Vienna](/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), Austria, after Switzerland declined to extend [diplomatic privileges](/wiki/Diplomatic_privileges "Diplomatic privileges").[[46]](#cite_note-46) At the time, Switzerland was attempting to reduce their foreign population and the OPEC was the first intergovernmental body to leave the country because of restrictions on foreigners.[[47]](#cite_note-47) Austria was keen to attract international organizations and offered attractive terms to the OPEC.[[48]](#cite_note-48)

During the early years of OPEC, the oil-producing countries had a 50/50 profit agreement with the oil companies.[[49]](#cite_note-FOOTNOTEColgan2021The_Rise_of_OPEC,_pp.

Thistletown Collegiate Institute :: History :: chunk_0001
Thistletown's first school, made of one frame schoolhouse was opened in 1874 on the east side of Islington Av., just south of Albion Rd. It was moved eastward to Village Green in 1901. The school expanded to reflect the growth in the village. In 1947, the [Etobicoke Board of Education](/wiki/Etobicoke_Board_of_Education "Etobicoke Board of Education") was established and a new building was built. The school was renamed to Thistletown Middle School.[[1]](#cite_note-1)

Construction of the current school began in 1956, and its first students were admitted in September 1957 as Etobicoke's seventh secondary school. The late 1960s brought expansions to technical and vocational facilities.

Thistletown Collegiate is a white-bricked, two-story 167,273-square-foot (15,540 m2) secondary school on a 14.5-acre campus. The main entrance is located on the second level.

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/dc/Adolf_Hitler_cropped_restored.jpg/250px-Adolf_Hitler_cropped_restored.jpg)](/wiki/File:Adolf_Hitler_cropped_restored.jpg)

[Adolf Hitler](/wiki/Adolf_Hitler "Adolf Hitler") led Germany during World War II.

Hitler exercised tight control over the German war effort, spending much of his time in his command bunkers (most notably at [Rastenburg](/wiki/Rastenburg "Rastenburg") in East Prussia, at [Vinnitsa](/wiki/Vinnitsa "Vinnitsa") in Ukraine, and under the garden of the [Reich Chancellery](/wiki/Reich_Chancellery "Reich Chancellery") in Berlin). At crucial periods in the war he held daily situation-conferences at which he used his remarkable talent for public speaking to overwhelm opposition from his generals and from the OKW staff with rhetoric.

In part because of the unexpected degree of German success in the Battle of France (despite the warnings of the professional military) Hitler believed himself a military genius, with a grasp of the total war effort that eluded his generals. In August 1941, when [Walther von Brauchitsch](/wiki/Walther_von_Brauchitsch "Walther von Brauchitsch") (commander-in-chief of the *Wehrmacht*) and Fedor von Bock appealed for an attack on Moscow, Hitler instead ordered the encirclement and capture of Ukraine, in order to acquire the farmland, industry, and natural resources of that country. Some historians like Bevin Alexander in *How Hitler Could Have Won* regard this decision as a missed opportunity to win the war.

In the winter of 1941–1942 Hitler believed that his obstinate refusal to allow the German armies to retreat had saved Army Group Centre from collapse. He later told [Erhard Milch](/wiki/Erhard_Milch "Erhard Milch"):

Each World Marathon Majors series originally spanned two full calendar years; the second year of a series overlapped with the first year of the next. Starting in 2015, each series began with a defined city race and ended with the following race in the same city. So, series IX started in February 2015 at the [2015 Tokyo Marathon](/wiki/2015_Tokyo_Marathon "2015 Tokyo Marathon") and ended there in February 2016 at the [2016 Tokyo Marathon](/wiki/2016_Tokyo_Marathon "2016 Tokyo Marathon"). Series X started at the [2016 Boston Marathon](/wiki/2016_Boston_Marathon "2016 Boston Marathon") and finished at the [2017 Boston Marathon](/wiki/2017_Boston_Marathon "2017 Boston Marathon"). Series XI started at the [2017 London Marathon](/wiki/2017_London_Marathon "2017 London Marathon") and finished at the [2018 London Marathon](/wiki/2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon").

Initial major sponsor [Abbott Laboratories](/wiki/Abbott_Laboratories "Abbott Laboratories") added its name in 2015.[[2]](#cite_note-Abbott-2) On April 26, 2017, Dalian Wanda Group Co., Ltd., one of the leading Chinese private conglomerates, announced a ten-year strategic partnership aimed at the continued growth and development of marathon events worldwide.

Beginning with Series X at the 2016 Boston Marathon, wheelchair competitions were added for men and women.

At the end of each of the first 10 WMM series the leading man and woman each won $500,000, making a total prize of one million U.S. dollars. Beginning with Series XI, the prize structure was revised so that for men and women first place became $250,000, second place $50,000 and third place $25,000. The university quickly established itself as a global leader in the study of mathematics. The university's examination in mathematics, known as the [Mathematical Tripos](/wiki/Mathematical_Tripos "Mathematical Tripos"),[[27]](#cite_note-28) was initially compulsory for all undergraduates studying for the Bachelor of Arts degree, the most common degree first offered at Cambridge. From the time of [Isaac Newton](/wiki/Isaac_Newton "Isaac Newton") in the late 17th century until the mid-19th century, the university maintained an especially strong emphasis on [applied mathematics](/wiki/Applied_mathematics "Applied mathematics"), and especially [mathematical physics](/wiki/Mathematical_physics "Mathematical physics"). Students awarded [first class honours](/wiki/British_undergraduate_degree_classification "British undergraduate degree classification") after completing the mathematics Tripos exam are called [wranglers](/wiki/Wrangler_(University_of_Cambridge) "Wrangler (University of Cambridge)"), and the top student among them is known as the [Senior Wrangler](/wiki/Senior_Wrangler "Senior Wrangler"), a position that has been described as "the greatest intellectual achievement attainable in Britain."[[28]](#cite_note-Forfar_1996-29)

The Cambridge Mathematical Tripos is highly competitive and has helped produce some of the most famous names in British science, including [James Clerk Maxwell](/wiki/James_Clerk_Maxwell "James Clerk Maxwell"), [Lord Kelvin](/wiki/William_Thomson,_1st_Baron_Kelvin "William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin"), and [Lord Rayleigh](/wiki/John_William_Strutt,_3rd_Baron_Rayleigh "John William Strutt, 3rd Baron Rayleigh").[[29]](#cite_note-30) However, some famous students

Main article: [Thyroid cancer](/wiki/Thyroid_cancer "Thyroid cancer")

A 2009 review found that alcohol intake does not affect the risk of developing thyroid cancer.[[160]](#cite_note-160) However, a 2009 study of 490,000 men and women concluded that alcohol may reduce the risk of thyroid cancer.[[161]](#cite_note-161) A 2009 study of 1,280,296 women in the United Kingdom concluded, "The decreased risk for thyroid cancer that we find to be associated with alcohol intake is consistent with results from some studies, although a meta-analysis of 10 case–control studies and two other cohort studies reported no statistically significant associations."[[47]](#cite_note-pmid19244173-47)

Main article: [Vaginal cancer](/wiki/Vaginal_cancer "Vaginal cancer")

A Danish study found that "Abstinence from alcohol consumption was associated with low risk for both VV-SCCvagina and VV-SCCvulva in our study."[[162]](#cite_note-Madsen-162)

A study concluded that alcoholic women are at high risk for cancer of the vagina.[[150]](#cite_note-Weiderpass-150) In both studies, indirect, lifestyle-related reasons were cited.

Main article: [Vulvar cancer](/wiki/Vulvar_cancer "Vulvar cancer")

One study reported "No consistent association emerged between milk, meat, liver, alcohol and coffee consumption and risk of vulvar cancer."[[163]](#cite_note-163) A Danish study found the reverse, that alcohol consumption is significantly associated with VV-SCCvagina and VV-SCCvulva cancer.[[162]](#cite_note-Madsen-162) A Swedish study concluded that alcoholic women are at no higher risk for cancer of the vulva.[[150]](#cite_note-Weiderpass-150)

Main article: [ThinkPad](/wiki/ThinkPad "ThinkPad")

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/45/Lenovo_ThinkPad_X1_Ultrabook.jpg/250px-Lenovo_ThinkPad_X1_Ultrabook.jpg)](/wiki/File:Lenovo_ThinkPad_X1_Ultrabook.jpg)

The first generation [ThinkPad X1](/wiki/ThinkPad_X1_series "ThinkPad X1 series") Carbon from 2012 Ultrabook with extensive use of lightweight and durable carbon fibre technology[[90]](#cite_note-90)[[91]](#cite_note-91)

The ThinkPad is a line of business-oriented [laptop](/wiki/Laptop "Laptop") known for their boxy black design, modeled after a traditional Japanese *[bento](/wiki/Bento "Bento")*.[[92]](#cite_note-92) The ThinkPad was originally an [IBM](/wiki/IBM "IBM") product developed at the [Yamato Facility](/wiki/IBM_Yamato_Facility "IBM Yamato Facility") in Japan by Arimasa Naitoh (内藤在正, *Naitō Arimasa*);[[93]](#cite_note-93) they have since been developed, manufactured and sold by both IBM and Lenovo after early 2005, following its acquisition of IBM's [personal computer](/wiki/Personal_computer "Personal computer") division. The ThinkPad has been used in space and was the only laptop model certified for use on the [International Space Station](/wiki/International_Space_Station "International Space Station") until 2016.[[94]](#cite_note-94)[[95]](#cite_note-95)
